Date: 2026-01-22
Time: 16:00 UTC

Attendees: Alex Martin, Priya Nair, Jonah Lee (Redwood) -- Daniel Reed, Maya Chen, Luis Ortega, Sophia Park (HelixVault)
Recording: Fireflies auto-transcript (unedited)
summary: Deep technical session to compare hotpath behavior between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM on HelixVault workloads. Focus areas: kernel selection and fallback, CUDA graph stability, persistent KV cache behavior with long-tail sequences, batching strategies for mixed-latency SLAs, and on-prem/VPC constraints (NVLink, NUMA). Agreed next steps to run targeted micro-benchmarks and an on-prem pilot.
topics: kernel selection; cuda graphs vs dynamic execution; persistent KV cache eviction patterns; batching algorithms (static, dynamic, time-window); quantization (fp16, int8, q4_0 style); VPC/on-prem networking & KMS; multi-gpu NVLink tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Martin: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're here to walk through runtime hotpath behavior, specifically TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM with your real traffic shapes, and the on-prem constraints you mentioned. Uh, Priya will lead most of the perf stuff.
[00:22] Daniel Reed: Thanks Alex. We're mostly worried about p95 latency spikes and token cost, and we also need to keep our KV cache across restarts for conversational context, so those are the priorities.
[00:35] Priya Nair: Cool. Before I start, quick confirmation — are you targeting single-GPU with NVLink or multi-node?
[00:42] Maya Chen: Initially single node, two GPUs with NVLink. We also need to consider NUMA on our racks, and the ops team prefers pinned CPU affinity.
[00:52] Priya: Got it. I'll call out NUMA effects; they change CUDA-graph allocation behavior.
[01:10] Jonah Lee: Quick note: we saw in our internal tests that TensorRT-LLM uses highly optimized fused kernels for some attention patterns which give lower p50, but vLLM's I/O and batching pipeline sometimes gives better tail latency under mixed request sizes.
[01:30] Maya: Can you explain why that divergence happens?
[01:36] Priya: Sure— TensorRT's fused kernels reduce kernel launch overhead and can exploit Tensor Cores aggressively, especially in fp16 or int8 quant modes. But it's less flexible when request shapes vary — if you have many short sequences, cudagraph replay of a fixed graph can be great or brittle depending on opcode variability. vLLM's path is more dynamic: it leans on smaller kernels and a scheduler that can re-batch at runtime, which reduces wasted tokens in some mixes.
[02:05] Daniel: So TensorRT wins on throughput for homogeneous long sequences?
[02:10] Priya: Typically yes. For long-transforms, when the sequence length is predictable, TRT fused kernels shine. For mixed short+long, vLLM's dynamic batching keeps the cost lower and sometimes improves p95 because it avoids padding inflation.
[02:28] [crosstalk] Alex: Another dimension is KV persistence — we've seen eviction patterns cause big variance. Priya, can you show our KV cache behavior slide?
[02:40] Priya: Yeah, so we instrumented a run with persistent KV caching enabled. When GPU memory gets high, CUDA allocator evicts noncritical buffers and if the runtime doesn't checkpoint the KV cache externally you'll hit recompute overheads. A bunch of vendors call this 'KV spill' or 'K V cash' in noisy transcripts, uh.
[03:05] Luis Ortega: In our stack we can't tolerate a full recompute on 10% of requests; it's unacceptable for user-facing chat. We prefer N seconds of degraded latency over full recompute.
[03:18] Priya: Right — so options: 1) persist KV to pinned CPU memory and prefetch before the next token, 2) tune eviction thresholds and batching policies to keep KV resident, or 3) use a smaller quantized KV representation to save GPU RAM at the cost of some quality.
[03:40] Maya: Number 1 sounds viable but prefetch costs network cycles in a VPC. Any numbers?
[03:46] Priya: From our microbenchmarks, prefetch from CPU pinned memory was ~8-12ms per prefetch on our test hardware; from NVMe-backed spill it was 50-120ms depending on IOPS. Prefetch into GPU via async memcpy overlapped with compute usually hides about half of that for long sequences.
[04:10] Daniel: What about CUDA graphs — are we using them in TRT always?
[04:15] Priya: TRT uses graph replay where possible to reduce launch overhead, but graph replay requires consistent agent execution paths. If your prompt routing or tool calls cause branching, the replay becomes invalid and you pay for graph re-recording which is expensive. vLLM doesn't rely on graph replay as heavily; it optimizes the scheduling layers instead.
[04:36] Alex: Important to call out: graph stability drops when you have function-calling or tool plugins that change the forward path per request.
[04:43] Sophia Park: From security side, we also need reproducible telemetry for audits. Does graph replay affect traceability?
[04:50] Jonah: Not inherently, but it can make per-inference instrumentation coarser if low-level kernel reuse hides intermediate ops. We add tracing hooks at the runtime boundary; you still get latency and token counts.
[05:05] [00:05:00-ish mark] Priya: I'll walk through a sample micro-benchmark we ran with a 7B model, fp16 vs int8-ish quant. Results: fp16 TRT p50=18ms p95=54ms; vLLM p50=24ms p95=60ms on uniform 512 tokens. On mixed traffic (50% short <64 tokens, 50% long 512), TRT p95 shot to 120ms because of graph re-recording and kernel mismatch, vLLM stayed around 72ms because dynamic re-batching compacted short requests.
[05:35] Maya: Did you try persistent KV on those runs?
[05:38] Priya: Yes, with persistent KV resident in GPU, TRT p95 for mixed improved to ~82ms — but memory pressure was high and we had occasional OOMs on synthetic spikes.
[05:50] Daniel: How about quantization quality? We're sensitive to hallucination rate.
[05:55] Priya: int8 reduced memory by ~40% and improved throughput, but we saw a measurable delta on long-form generation quality on our eval prompts — roughly a 2-3% ROUGE-ish regression on the set you shared with us. q4-style 4-bit heuristics gave a middle ground: decent memory saving with smaller quality drop.
[06:20] Luis: Could we hybridize — e.g., keep KV in fp16 but model tensors in q4?
[06:25] Priya: Yes — hybrid approaches are common. Keep critical KV at higher fidelity and quantize large weight matrices. That adds engineering complexity but good tradeoff.
[06:35] Alex: Let's talk about batching strategies. Static batch fills with padding — good for accel but hurts short-request users. Dynamic batching groups by sequence length/windows which needs a low-latency scheduler.
[06:50] Priya: Our runtime offers several policies: fixed-size batching, time-window batching (X ms wait to fill), shape-based bucketing, and priority lanes. For HelixVault with mixed SLAs, we recommend a two-lane approach: a fast-lane for short interactive requests (small batch, low wait) and a throughput-lane for long background generations (larger batch, cudagraph-friendly).
[07:12] Maya: Does Redwood runtime support automatic lane fallback when load shifts?
[07:16] Priya: Yes — we have automatic routing policies that move model variants or routes by latency tier. We can also fall back from TRT to vLLM-compatible kernels if graph instability crosses a threshold.
[07:28] Daniel: Tell me about kernel fallback cost — is switching on the fly expensive?
[07:32] Priya: Switching kernels involves bringing a different set of modules into GPU memory; that can cost hundreds of milliseconds if you reload weights. We mitigate via warm pools and preloading candidates into memory when capacity allows. We also support smaller model variants as fallback to avoid weight load costs.
[07:48] Jonah: NVLink considerations — if you split KV across two GPUs, NVLink moves KV faster than PCIe but synchronization and cross-gpu atomics add latency. On some workloads we co-locate model partitions and KV to avoid cross-GPU fetches.
[08:05] Sophia: From a security perspective, on-prem deployment with your private control plane — how do you integrate customer KMS?
[08:11] Alex: We integrate with customer-managed HSM/KMS via a connector; keys never leave the VPC. We can provide audit logs and escrowed attestation for compliance. We'll share SOC2 docs as requested.
[08:25] Maya: Great. Back to observability — what traces and counters should we expect?
[08:30] Priya: You get token-level latency, per-kernel durations (best-effort), batch composition stats, cache hit/miss rates, memory pressure events, and CUDA graph replay counts. For on-prem we can send metrics to your Prometheus or our console depending on your retention choice.
[08:48] Daniel: Could you run a benchmark that simulates our exact distribution — short interactive queries (60% median <32 tokens) and long generative jobs (40% 512+ tokens) — and show both TRT and vLLM with persistent KV?
[08:58] Priya: Absolutely. We already have a harness; we'll plug your prompt set. A couple clarifying questions: do you want quality-anchored runs (same quant+model) or cost-anchored runs (best config per runtime)?
[09:12] Daniel: Start with quality-anchored (same model fp16) so we can isolate runtime differences, then a cost-anchored pass.
[09:20] Priya: Perfect. We'll also include a run with graph replay forced-off to see impact.
[09:25] Luis: About network and prefetch — in VPC how much overhead should we budget for pinned-CPU prefetch? We have 100 Gbps interconnects and decent NICs.
[09:33] Priya: With 100Gbps and low NIC latency, our observed prefetch times from host pinned mem into GPU were in single-digit ms ranges when not contended. But if your cluster is noisy and the OS swaps, it's more. That's where NUMA and proper CPU pinning matter.
[09:51] Maya: We're going to provision dedicated nodes for this pilot to reduce noisy neighbor.
[09:56] Alex: That helps a lot. Also worth noting: persistent KV plus quantization often hits an inflection point where you can drop to a single-GPU serving more requests per card, but you must measure hallucination/quality curves at your prompt set.
[10:15] [10:15 mark] Priya: Quick demo: I'll read out an excerpt from our internal run logs — you'll see kernel durations: attention_fused_kernel (TRT) 7.2ms, matmul_chunk_n (vLLM) 3.4ms but called more often; cuda_graph_replay_count went from 0 to 9 in the mixed workload which triggered re-recording overheads.
[10:40] Daniel: Those re-records are the big surprise. Can we proactively detect path variability and switch to a dynamic mode before re-recording?
[10:46] Priya: Yes — heuristics detect branching and we can switch to a dynamic trace-less path if instability crosses thresholds; that reduces re-recording but raises p50 slightly. It's a configurable tradeoff.
[11:00] Luis: For pilot acceptance criteria: p95 < 200ms for interactive lane, p50 < 60ms for throughput lane, cost per 1k tokens within X (we'll define after we see numbers). Can Redwood instrument cost breakdowns per-token?
[11:13] Alex: Yes — we deliver token-level cost estimates and you can map them to routes and models. We'll include a breakdown in the micro-benchmark spreadsheet.
[11:24] Sophia: Security follow-up — will you provide docs for on-prem agent hardening and SAML SSO for console?
[11:30] Alex: Yes, we have hardening guides and SAML/SSO integration docs. We'll drop those into the shared drive.
[11:40] Daniel: Any gotchas about NUMA + CUDA graphs you want to call out?
[11:45] Priya: Yes — if GPU DMA crosses NUMA boundaries to staged CPU memory it can increase copy latencies by 2-3x. Keep pinned buffers on the same NUMA node as the GPU. Also watch kernel launch time variance under heavy interrupts.
[11:59] Maya: Noted.
[12:05] [Wrap-up, final 2 minutes] Alex: Quick recap — Redwood to run quality-anchored TRT vs vLLM microbenchmarks with your prompt set, include runs: persistent KV in GPU, persistent KV in pinned host mem, graph on/off, quant modes (fp16, q4, int8). Priya will lead perf artifacts. We'll schedule an on-prem pilot week, pre-provisioned nodes, and Sophia will get security docs. Any final questions?
[12:27] Daniel: No, that covers it. Thanks.
[12:30] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links and timeline.

Note: transcript contains occasional mis-attributions and ASR artifacts (e.g., 'K V cash' for KV cache).
